# GPT 6.1 Sol xhigh as the main technical reviewer (2026-09-29 to 2026-10-02)

**Goal.** GPT 6.1 Sol became available, and the user asked for an evaluation of how close it is to Opus 5.5, run at xhigh. The eval started on the boundary-hunter role; partway through, the user redirected it to the main technical review and stopped the hunter work. Part 1 answers how close GPT 6.1 Sol xhigh is to Opus 5.5 xhigh as the main technical reviewer, and how it compares with GPT 6 Sol xhigh. The user then asked for up to 10 prompt iterations to bring GPT 6.1 closer to Opus; Part 2 reports that tuning and a blind check of the result on unseen PRs. The stopped hunter work is summarised at the end.

## Headline

- **Part 1, untuned.** GPT 6.1 Sol xhigh is accurate but found fewer issues than Opus 5.5 xhigh as the main reviewer: 27 against 32 of 36 VALID items, and a mean rank of 2.0 against 1.2.
- **Part 2, tuned.** A 443-word task prompt (`tune/prompts/v10.md`) roughly doubled GPT 6.1's VALID findings on untouched validation PRs (16 against 8). On five unseen PRs judged blind three ways, it found more than Opus (20 against Opus's 17 and the untuned model's 17). Opus still ranked first on 4 of 5, on calibration.
- **Part 3, bold structures.** Five completely different ways of running the review (author defense, contract first, ensemble with a verifying merge, decomposed lenses, conclusion first) did not clearly beat the pinned v10 prompt. The closest, decomposed lenses, met the calibration bar by one PR and costs about eight times as much.
- **Part 4, native harness.** Running GPT 6.1 Sol in the Codex CLI instead of Pi made no measurable difference to quality (0, +1 and +1 VALID over 5 PRs for untuned, v10 and E5). The prompt is what matters: Codex with v10 found 20 of 24 VALID items, ranked best of seven (Opus included) and cost $1.65 per PR against $2.25 for Pi with v10.

# Part 1: untuned GPT 6.1 Sol as main reviewer (2026-09-29)

## Result in one table

10 PRs, 36 VALID issues in the verified pool. Judges scored all three reports per PR blind.

| Main reviewer | VALID found (of 36) | Partial | Unique VALID | WRONG findings | False claims | Recommendation justified | Mean rank (1 best) | Ranked first | Min/PR | List cost/PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opus 5.5 xhigh | **32** | 3 | **7** | 1 | 0 | **9/10** | **1.2** | 8 | 22.3 | $5.59 |
| GPT 6.1 Sol xhigh | 27 | 7 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 5/10 | 2.0 | 1 | 22.1 | $1.39 |
| GPT 6 Sol xhigh | 22 | 6 | 1 | 2 | 1 | 4/10 | 2.8 | 1 | 9.1 | $1.11 |

The one WRONG finding shared by Opus and GPT 6.1 was made by all three reviewers (12167, see below).

**Answer:**
- **GPT 6.1 is not yet a substitute for Opus as the main reviewer.** It found 27 of the 36 VALID issues against Opus's 32. It found no VALID issue that Opus missed, while Opus found 7 that nobody else did. Its overall recommendation was justified in 5 of 10 PRs against 9 of 10 for Opus.
- **It is accurate.** It made no false claims, and its only WRONG finding is one that all three reviewers shared.
- **Against GPT 6, it is better on the held-out set and about level on the fresh set.** The fresh-set comparison is the fairer one (see Caveats).
- **It costs a quarter of Opus's list price** ($1.39 against $5.59 per PR) at the same wall time (about 22 min). It takes more than twice as long as GPT 6.

## Method

- **PRs.** Two sets of 5, 10 in total:
  - Held-out: 12425, 12535, 12232, 12538 and 12167, from batch `v3-200-20260924`, the same PRs as `evals/sol-hunter-validation-20260927`.
  - Fresh: 13575, 13540, 13412, 13546 and 13585, from batch `v3-200-20260928`. They were reviewed and published there, and no earlier eval or prompt tuning used them.
- **Opus 5.5 xhigh baseline.** The production Opus reviewer's first-pass report for each PR (`opus/final.md`, or `final-report.md` where that is the only one). These reports were written before any coordinator follow-up, from the same brief. No new Opus reviews were run.
- **GPT 6 Sol xhigh baseline.**
  - On the held-out set, GPT 6 was production's independent second reviewer: its first-pass `sol/final.md`, run 1 of its job.
  - On the fresh set, production used GPT 6 as the boundary hunter instead. So this eval ran it in `pi_job`'s standard review mode, the same way as GPT 6.1.
- **GPT 6.1 Sol xhigh.** `pi_job.py start --provider openai-codex --model gpt-6.1-sol --thinking xhigh` in the default review mode, with the production `reviewer.md` system prompt and the PR's own brief.
  - Every run passed `pi_job.py verify`: `reply_models` is only `gpt-6.1-sol` (or `gpt-6-sol`), and `thinking_levels` is only `xhigh`. No run fell back.
  - At most 2 Sol jobs ran at a time, and the Codex account reported no rate-limit errors.
- **Clean inputs.** The production assignment folders now hold the published reviews. So the new runs worked from copies:
  - `setup_heldout.py`: the brief, the pre-review intake and the pinned worktrees, with git pointers re-aimed at the copy. It leaves out coordinator files, post-review snapshots and the other reviewers' output.
  - `setup_fresh.py`: fresh blobless clones re-pinned to each brief's recorded head, merge-base and `quattro` commits.
  - After all runs, `git status` was clean in every pinned worktree.
- **Blind judging** (`JUDGE-REVIEW.md`, one Opus judge per PR):
  - `blind_review.py` copied the three reports under anonymous ids, with model names, runtime names and output-folder prefixes redacted and absolute paths cut to their last component.
  - Each judge built a findings pool from the three reports and verified every item against the pinned source. Items were classed VALID, MINOR or WRONG, using the earlier judges' rules for weak tests and cross-PR items.
  - Judges also checked each report's 5 or more most load-bearing positive claims, rated the recommendation and severities, and ranked the reports.
- **Totals.** Unblinded by `totals.py` into `scores-review/unblinded-totals.json`. Time and cost are in `costs-review.json` (`cost_review.py`).
  - Sol costs are list-price token costs from the Pi session logs, counting only the first run.
  - Opus costs come from the production reviewer's transcript up to the report's write time, priced at $4 input, $20 output, $0.20 cache read and $8 cache write per million tokens. These rates reproduce `total_cost_usd` for 9 recorded `claude -p` Opus 5.5 runs to within $0.0001.

## Results per set

**Held-out (5 PRs, 20 VALID):**

| | VALID found | Partial | Unique | WRONG findings / false claims | Justified | Mean rank |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opus 5.5 xhigh | 20 | 0 | 5 | 1 / 0 | 5/5 | 1.0 |
| GPT 6.1 Sol xhigh | 15 | 3 | 0 | 1 / 0 | 3/5 | 2.0 |
| GPT 6 Sol xhigh (production run) | 9 | 5 | 0 | 2 / 1 | 3/5 | 3.0 |

**Fresh (5 PRs, 16 VALID):**

| | VALID found | Partial | Unique | WRONG findings / false claims | Justified | Mean rank |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opus 5.5 xhigh | 12 | 3 | 2 | 0 / 0 | 4/5 | 1.4 |
| GPT 6.1 Sol xhigh | 12 | 4 | 0 | 0 / 0 | 2/5 | 2.0 |
| GPT 6 Sol xhigh (eval run) | 13 | 1 | 1 | 0 / 0 | 1/5 | 2.6 |

The fresh-set VALID counts are nearly even. Opus still ranked first on 3 of 5 PRs. The judges' reasons were mainly calibration: the right severity and a justified recommendation, rather than presenting minor edge cases as blocking. They also credited Opus's deeper executed evidence, such as mutants and fix controls.

## Per-PR notes

- **12425** (agent limit-reset toasts)
  - Opus found all 5 VALID issues. It was the only reviewer to find that `omarchy bar set ... false` stores the string "false", which keeps the feature on, and that the disable test only exercises a dead path.
  - GPT 6.1 found the three main integration defects (per-monitor duplicate toasts, Do Not Disturb bypass, no re-queue on re-enable), backed by executed evidence.
  - GPT 6 found none of them.
- **12535** (upgrade retargeting after master removal)
  - Opus alone found that the saved upstream change is lost when the fast-forward pull fails on the diverged final master.
  - GPT 6.1 was partial on that issue, but had the widest edge-case matrix. GPT 6 missed it.
- **12232** (wind in m/s)
  - All three found the mph notification mismatch and the missing opt-out.
  - Only Opus raised the untested QML wiring as a finding.
- **12538** (idle timeouts of 0)
  - Opus and GPT 6.1 found both VALID issues; GPT 6 was partial.
  - GPT 6 was the only reviewer to spot the one variant new in this PR (screensaver set to 0 makes the lock arrive early). It also made the only WRONG finding on this PR, a claim about `screensaverTimer`.
- **12167** (audit rules)
  - Opus alone found the most material issue: audit is a hard dependency of Arch systemd and pam, so the PR turns kernel auditing on for every install.
  - All three wrongly claimed a missing `/etc/ssh` breaks the rule load. It cannot be missing, because gnome-keyring pulls in openssh.
  - GPT 6 also made a false claim that audit userspace may be absent.
- **13575** (sudo keepalive)
  - All three found that an in-flight `sudo -n true` can undo the exit revoke.
  - Only Opus showed, with mutants, that the shipped defaults are never tested. GPT 6.1 was partial on that point.
- **13540** (hibernate on critical battery)
  - Opus and GPT 6.1 found both VALID issues (no migration for existing installs, and the fresh-setup path is untested). GPT 6 was partial on the test gap.
  - GPT 6.1 ranked below Opus for over-weighting minor failure-handling cases.
- **13412** (Dropbox status)
  - All three found the three VALID issues ("Syncing paused" shown as syncing, a full folder walk on every poll that also drops pause clicks, and a pulse that ignores reduced motion).
  - GPT 6.1 ranked first, presenting all three as confirmed findings with fixes. Opus left the first as a hypothesis.
- **13546** (localized dates)
  - GPT 6 ranked first. It was the only reviewer with all 6 VALID issues, including the mixed native-digit output for ar_EG.
  - Opus missed that issue. GPT 6.1 treated it and the English word order only as open questions.
- **13585** (GDK scale at first run)
  - Opus alone found the lid-shut docked case, where the disabled HiDPI panel is not counted and scale 1 is written permanently.
  - GPT 6.1 was partial on it. GPT 6 missed it.

## Caveats

- **Sample size.** 10 PRs and 36 VALID items. A difference of one or two issues is noise, but the ranking pattern is consistent: Opus had a mean rank of 1.2 and ranked first 8 times.
- **The held-out comparison with GPT 6 is not like for like:**
  - GPT 6's held-out reports are production runs from 2026-09-25, made under the `reviewer.md` of that time. `reviewer.md` changed on 2026-09-28 when bwrap was removed.
  - GPT 6.1 ran on 2026-09-29 with the current prompt.
  - On the fresh set, both Sol models ran the same day with the same prompt and inputs, and they were about level on recall.
  - So the large held-out gap (15 against 9) is partly a prompt and runtime effect, not only a model effect.
- **Opus baselines are production reports.** They were run as the Claude Code `omarchy-reviewer` subagent. The Sol runs used `pi_job`. This mirrors production, which is what a switch would change.
- **Blinding is imperfect.**
  - Report length differs: Opus about 2,300 to 3,400 words, GPT 6.1 about 2,200 to 3,400, GPT 6 about 700 to 1,500. So only GPT 6's reports are easy to tell apart.
  - Judges were told to ignore style, but depth of evidence is legitimately part of the score.
- **Our reviews of these PRs are public on GitHub.** The Sol runs worked from clean copies, and their instructions forbid reading PR comments. A later audit of every run log (Part 2) found that the GPT 6.1 run on 13412 fetched the live PR comments in a final "freshness check" and read our published review. It did so after its findings were written, used one MINOR wrapping note from it as a lead, and disclosed this in its report. Its ranking on 13412 (first) is therefore not fully independent; no other Part 1 run read the discussion.

## Recommendation

1. **Keep Opus 5.5 xhigh as the main technical reviewer.** GPT 6.1 at xhigh is closer to it than GPT 6 is, but it found 27 of the 36 VALID issues against Opus's 32, and it never found one that Opus missed. Its overall recommendation was justified half as often as Opus's. Switching would save about $4.20 of Claude usage per PR at list price, with no change in wall time.
2. **If Claude usage becomes the binding constraint**, GPT 6.1 xhigh is the best fallback main reviewer measured so far. It was accurate (no false claims) and ranked first or second on 9 of 10 PRs. It is better than GPT 6 as a main reviewer, clearly so on the held-out set and slightly on the fresh set (rank 2.0 against 2.6).
3. **Not measured here: GPT 6.1 as the boundary hunter**, the role GPT 6 holds in production. The hunter comparison was stopped at the user's request before it produced scores. A switch in that role should be decided on its own eval.
4. **Production suggestion, not applied:** keep the second technical opinion (Sol) in the pipeline. On 13546 GPT 6 found a VALID issue that Opus missed. On 12538 and 13412 a Sol reviewer had the sharper analysis of an issue both found. That is the case for keeping two independent reviewers.

# Part 2: prompt tuning of GPT 6.1 Sol as main reviewer (2026-09-30)

**Goal.** Find what it takes, by prompting alone, to bring GPT 6.1 Sol xhigh closer to Opus 5.5 xhigh as the main reviewer: form hypotheses, test each, at most 10 iterations. The full log is `tune/LOG.md`; prompts are in `tune/prompts/`.

## Method

- **Where the prompt goes.** Each version is a task file passed with `pi_job.py start --task`, on top of the unchanged production `reviewer.md` system prompt and the PR's own brief. No production file was changed.
- **Tuning set:** 12425, 12167, 13575, 13585, 13546, the five Part 1 PRs where GPT 6.1 had the most headroom. Every version ran once on all five.
- **Validation set:** 12535, 12232, 12538, 13540, 13412, untouched while tuning.
- **Final check:** five PRs no part of this eval had used: 13542, 13533, 13526, 13405, 13569, from batch `v3-200-20260928`, re-pinned under `fresh/`.
- **Paired blind judging** (`tune/JUDGE-TUNE.md`). Each tuned report was judged against the untuned GPT 6.1 report of the same PR, as anonymous P and Q, against the verified Part 1 pool (`tune/pool/`), with new issues verified against the pinned source. Because both reports share one judge, judge leniency cancels out. The baseline scored 13 or 14 of the tuning pool in every judgement, matching Part 1.
- **Final check judging.** A blind three-way judgement (`JUDGE-REVIEW.md`) of the production Opus first-pass report, untuned GPT 6.1 and tuned GPT 6.1 (v10), with a pool built from scratch.
- **Pools grew.** Judges confirmed new VALID items, for example tests that still pass with the feature wiring deleted. These were added to `tune/pool/` between rounds. Paired differences are unaffected.

## Diagnosis that set the direction

On 8 of 10 Part 1 PRs, untuned GPT 6.1 saw the evidence behind an issue it then missed or only half found. It noted the observation and stopped, or reasoned from the right fact in the wrong direction. Examples:

- **12167:** it saw that audit is always installed, but used that only to rule out a missing-package bug, and missed that the PR therefore turns kernel auditing on for everyone.
- **13585:** it saw that disabled outputs are excluded, and called that "not a confirmed bug".
- **12425:** it found that the documented CLI stores the string "false", and dismissed it as user error.
- **13546:** it filed two locale defects as "product questions".

Its second weakness was calibration.

## Iterations (tuning set, each paired with the untuned baseline)

| Version | Hypothesis | VALID found vs baseline | WRONG or false | Recommendation justified | Judged better | $/PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| v1 | Force every lead to a verdict | 12 vs 14 (-2) | 1 | 4/5 | 2/5 | 1.65 |
| v2 | Base comparison, mutation-test the PR's tests, severity by reachability | 17 vs 13 (+4) | 1 | 4/5 | 4/5 | 1.30 |
| v3 | Trace the change through the real system: premises, entry points and value shapes, fresh and existing installs, platform states, test reality | 19 vs 14 (+5) | 1 | 5/5 | 4/5 | 2.22 |
| v4 | Breadth first: at least 20 failure hypotheses before testing | 16 vs 14 (+2) | 2 | 5/5 | 4/5 | 2.19 |
| v5 | v3 + v2 | 20 vs 14 (+6) | 0 | 4/5 | 5/5 | 1.81 |
| v6 | v5 + claimed versus actual effect for each population | 21 vs 14 (+7) | 0 | 4/5 | 4/5 | 1.92 |
| v7 | v6 with severity anchored on the PR's own claims | 19 vs 14 (+5) | 0 | 5/5 | 5/5 | 1.63 |
| v8 | v7 in 340 words, no mandatory worksheet files | 21 vs 14 (+7) | 1 false claim | 5/5 | 5/5 | 1.67 |
| v9 | v7 + checks before dismissing a confirmed mechanism | 20 vs 14 (+6) | 0 | 4/5 | 5/5 | 2.06 |
| **v10** | **v8 + those dismissal checks + verify any fix advice (443 words)** | **19 vs 14 (+5)** | **0** | **5/5** | **5/5** | **1.79** |

The tuning pool held 21 to 25 VALID items as it grew. Runs are single samples; a difference of one or two issues is noise.

## What made the difference

1. **Tracing the change through the real system (v3, +5).** This was the largest single gain. Asking what each guard evaluates to on a real install, which exact value arrives from each documented entry point, and what fresh and existing installs each get, recovered issues that only Opus had found in Part 1: the CLI "false" string, the docked-laptop case and the missing migration.
2. **Opus's evidence habits (v2, +4).** Comparing with base, mutating the main change to test the PR's tests, and rating severity by who reaches it. This turned half-found test gaps into proven findings with named surviving mutants.
3. **The two together (v5, +6), then claimed versus actual effect (v6, +7).** v6 was the first version to find that 12167 turns on kernel auditing for every install, which only Opus had found.
4. **Calibration anchored on the PR's claims (v7).** v2's rule ("rare state means Low; Low-only means merge") over-corrected: v5 and v6 each recommended merging once where changes were due. Tying severity to what the PR says it delivers restored justified recommendations on all 5 PRs.
5. **Worksheets are not what matters (v8).** The same instructions in 340 words, without required worksheet files, scored as well as the 950-word version.
6. **What did not help:**
   - Forcing every lead to a verdict (v1). The model resolved its leads by inflating MINOR points, not by finding the missed issues.
   - Breadth-first hypothesis lists (v4). Many more MINOR items, few more VALID ones.
   - A longer dismissal checklist on the long prompt (v9). More cost, and one over-severe recommendation.

**Chosen:** v10 (`tune/prompts/v10.md`). v7, v8 and v10 are tied within noise. v10 is compact, and its check on fix advice removed v8's only false claim, a claim that would have reached a public comment.

## Validation on untouched PRs (paired with the untuned baseline)

| Prompt | VALID found vs baseline | Partial | WRONG or false | Recommendation justified | Judged better |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| v8 | 15 vs 9 (+6) | 2 vs 8 | 0 | 5 vs 4 | 5/5 |
| **v10** | **16 vs 8 (+8)** | 1 vs 9 | 0 | 4 vs 4 | 5/5 |

Both prompts generalize: on PRs never used in tuning they roughly double the untuned model's VALID findings and turn almost all its half-found issues into full findings. The validation pool grew by three judge-verified weak-test and state items along the way, which is why the baselines differ slightly (9 and 8).

## Final check: blind three-way on five unseen PRs

5 PRs, 23 VALID issues in the verified pool.

| Main reviewer | VALID found | Partial | Unique VALID | WRONG / false claims | Recommendation justified | Mean rank | Ranked first | Min/PR | List $/PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opus 5.5 xhigh (production reports) | 17 | 3 | 1 | 0 / 1 | 4/5 | **1.4** | **4** | 22.1 | 5.82 |
| **GPT 6.1 xhigh + v10** | **20** | 2 | **3** | 1 / 0 | 3/5 | 1.8 | 1 | 33.8 | 2.25 |
| GPT 6.1 xhigh, untuned | 17 | 3 | 1 | 1 / 0 | 4/5 | 2.8 | 0 | 31.6 | 1.38 |

- **13542, fingerprint setup.** All three found 4 of 5. Only Opus found the wrong "try enrolling again" advice.
- **13533, Tailscale.** Opus 6/7, both GPT runs 5/7. Opus ranked first for leading with the retry-refusal defect.
- **13526, zram migration.** Only v10 found both VALID items, including test stubs that ignore their arguments. It over-rated two items, so Opus ranked first. The untuned run did a boundary hunt instead of a main review.
- **13405, mute LED.** All three found both VALID items (the #13424 key path makes the fix inert on quattro; writing 0 removes the kernel trigger). Both GPT runs raised a localized-pactl finding that is WRONG on Omarchy, because libpulse ships no translations there.
- **13569, floating bar.** v10 found all 7 VALID items and ranked first. It was the only report to find the regression in the default docked bar. Opus found 4 and made a false "docked bar unchanged" claim.

**Reading.** On unseen PRs, the tuned prompt brought GPT 6.1 from Opus's level of recall to above it (20 against 17), with the most unique finds. It also moved GPT 6.1's mean rank from 2.8 to 1.8. Opus still ranked first on 4 of 5 PRs: the judges preferred its severity calibration and its choice of what to lead with. v10's remaining weakness is over-rating secondary items.

## Contamination found and fixed

- **What happened.** By the time these runs ran, our production reviews of the eval PRs were public. A log audit (`tune/scan_discussion.py`) found 3 of about 90 GPT runs that fetched the PR's live comments in a final "freshness check", despite instructions not to read PR discussion:
  - the Part 1 run on 13412 (see Part 1 caveats);
  - the final-check baseline on 13405;
  - v10 on 13526.
- **Fix.** Both final-check runs were set aside (`runs-interrupted/contaminated/`) and rerun with `tune/ghguard/gh` first on PATH. The guard refuses comment and review reads for the PR, logs any attempt, and changes no prompt.
- **After the fix.** All later runs were scanned clean, and the guard logged no attempts from reviewers.
- **Production relevance.** Production GPT runs happen before publication, so this does not affect production reviews. It does affect any evaluation that replays published PRs.

## Caveats

- **Single samples.** One run per version per PR. Run-to-run noise is about 1 to 2 VALID issues per 5-PR set, so v5 to v10 are statistically tied. The validation and final check are the evidence that the gain is real.
- **Opus judges.** All judges were Opus 5.5. Opus still ranked first on the final check while finding fewer issues. Judge preference for Opus's style cannot be ruled out, though every item was verified against source.
- **Leakage.** The tuning prompts use generic categories, and pool-specific examples were removed. The final-check PRs were never seen while tuning.
- **Runtime.** The GPT runs shared the Codex account with production and ran in daytime. Wall time rose to 34 to 45 min per PR while token cost barely moved, so treat runtime as load-dependent.
- **Opus baselines.** Opus is represented by production first-pass reports, not re-runs with a tuned prompt. Nobody tried to tune Opus.

## Recommendation (Part 2)

1. **Keep Opus 5.5 as the main reviewer for now.** It still ranks first most often, mainly on calibration and prioritization.
2. **Replace the production GPT 6 hunter with GPT 6.1 xhigh running `tune/prompts/v10.md` as a second full reviewer.** On unseen PRs it found more VALID issues than Opus, and 3 that nobody else found, at $2.25 per PR (about what the GPT 6 hunter's v11 single pass costs). Opus plus tuned GPT 6.1 covers more than either alone. The coordinator already triages severity, which covers v10's tendency to over-rate. This needs a production change (`pi_job.py start --task tune/prompts/v10.md --model gpt-6.1-sol`), which this eval did not make.
3. **If Claude usage becomes the binding constraint,** GPT 6.1 + v10 is now a credible main reviewer: its recall matches or beats Opus, at 39% of the cost. Keep a calibration pass (the coordinator's triage) on its severities and recommendation.
4. **For future evaluations on published PRs,** run GPT reviewers with the `gh` guard on PATH.

# Part 3: five bold experiments against pinned v10 (2026-10-01)

**Goal.** Recall, calibration and lead choice plateaued from v5 to v10. Part 3 freezes v10 as the control and tests up to five completely different ways of running the review, to see whether any of them moves the plateau. These are new structures, not more rules added to v10. The plan and thresholds were written before any run (`tune/PART3-PLAN.md`).

## Method

- **Control.** v10 is frozen read-only as `tune/prompts/v10-pinned.md`, with the same SHA-256 as `v10.md`. Its existing runs on the five final-check PRs (13542, 13533, 13526, 13405, 13569) are the control, so no new control runs were needed. Tuning never touched those PRs.
- **Experiments.** All five used GPT 6.1 Sol xhigh through `pi_job`, the production `reviewer.md` and the PR brief. Every run had the `gh` guard first on PATH and passed the run-log audit.

| Id | Idea | How it runs |
|---|---|---|
| E1 | Adversarial author defense | A v10 pass, then a second pass in the same session arguing as the PR author against every finding: keep, downgrade or drop, then re-rank |
| E2 | Contract first | Write the PR's claims, affected groups and must-not-change list before reading the diff, then judge the diff only against that contract |
| E3 | Independent ensemble plus a verifying merge | Two independent v10 runs, then a fresh session that verifies every disagreement and single-source finding, then merges and ranks |
| E4 | Decomposed lenses | One session, five passes: the PR's own logic, the rest of the system, tests, outside the diff, then a separate merge-and-rank pass |
| E5 | Conclusion first | Name the 1 to 3 must-know items and a provisional recommendation before any experiment, then spend the effort trying to overturn them |

- **Judging.** One blind judgement per PR covered every report: E1 to E5, pinned v10 and the Opus production report, under random letters (`tune/JUDGE-BOLD.md`). It scored against the verified Part 2 pool (23 VALID), recorded whether each report led with the most important issue, and ranked all seven. Where E4 finished last, it was scored by a small blind add-on judgement against the same pool and ranking (`tune/JUDGE-BOLD-ADDON.md`).
- **Pre-registered thresholds** (5 PRs, against v10 in the same judgements):
  - Recall moves at +4 VALID or more.
  - Calibration and lead move when at least two of three hold: ranked above Opus on 3 or more PRs, recommendation justified on 4 or more, and leading with the top issue on 2 or more PRs more than v10.
  - Guard: no more WRONG findings or false claims than v10.
  - A yes needs a confirmation run.

## Results

| Config | VALID found (of 23) | vs v10 | WRONG + false | Justified | Leads with top issue | Above Opus | Above v10 | Mean rank (of 7) | List $/PR | Wall time/PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| E1 author defense | 18 | 0 | 2 | 4 | 2 | 1 | 0 | 4.6 | 3.55 | 58 min |
| E2 contract first | 14 | -4 | 2 | 2 | 1 | 2 | 1 | 4.8 | 1.51 | 33 min |
| E3 ensemble plus merge | 17 | -1 | 1 | 3 | 3 | 2 | 0 | 4.0 | 4.76 | 52 min |
| E4 decomposed lenses | 17 | -1 | 1 | 4 | 4 | 3 | 3 | 3.0 | 17.43 | 3.5 h |
| E5 conclusion first | 17 | -1 | 1 | 4 | 3 | 1 | 2 | 3.8 | 1.28 | 26 min |
| **v10 pinned (control)** | **18** | | 1 | 3 | 3 | 2 | | **2.8** | 2.25 | 34 min |
| Opus 5.5 (production) | 15 | -3 | 2 | 4 | 3 | | 3 | 3.2 | 5.82 | 22 min |

VALID found and rank per PR:

| 13542 fingerprint (5) | 3, r6 | 3, r4 | 3, r7 | **5, r1** | 4, r3 | 3, r4 | 3, r2 |
| 13533 Tailscale (7) | 5, r3 | 2, r6 | 3, r4 | 4, r4 | 4, r4 | 4, r2 | **6, r1** |

| 13569 floating bar (7) | 6, r4 | 5, r5 | **7, r1** | 3, r6 | 5, r3 | **7, r1** | 3, r7 |

## What moved and what did not

- **Recall did not move.** No experiment beat pinned v10's 18 VALID. The best tied it (E1). The plateau is not a sampling effect:
  - E3 ran v10 twice independently and merged the results, yet found 17. Its verifying merge dropped or softened items one run had found.
  - E2 cost recall (-4) by narrowing the review to the PR's own claims.
- **E4 is the only experiment that met the calibration bar, and only by the narrowest margin.**
  - It ranked above Opus on 3 PRs and had a justified recommendation on 4, clearing each test by a single PR. Its lead-choice gain over v10 was +1 against the +2 required.
  - It was the strongest report on 13542 and 13526, but sixth on 13569, where it missed the default-bar regression that v10 found.
  - Its mean rank (3.0) is slightly worse than v10's (2.8), and it found one VALID item fewer.
  - It costs about 8 times v10 and 3 times Opus, and takes 3.5 hours per PR.

  Under the rule set before the runs this counts as a move needing confirmation. Under the stricter reading that a small, uncertain gain is a no, it is a no. The confirmation run (about 4 hours and about $90 list on Codex) was not run: the user declined it on 2026-10-02.
- **The other ideas did not help:**
  - E1 (author defense) kept v10's recall but added a false claim, so it fails the guard. The defense pass did not improve calibration.
  - E5 (conclusion first) is the cheapest ($1.28) and fastest configuration, at -1 VALID with no calibration gain.
  - E2 and E3 were behind v10.
- **A side result.** In this seven-way judging, pinned v10 ranked ahead of the Opus production reports (mean rank 2.8 against 3.2) and found more VALID issues (18 against 15). This agrees with the Part 2 final check on recall. Opus still had more justified recommendations (4 against 3).

## Process notes

- **Deviations approved by the user while running, both recorded with times in the plan's run notes:**
  - E4's chains got the first free Sol slot.
  - 13533 was judged without E4, which was added later by the add-on judgement.
- **The `gh` guard worked.** It refused three attempts to read an evaluated PR's own discussion: E1 on 13405, and E4's outside-the-diff pass on 13533 and 13526. Their saved files are empty, and the audit found no other route.
- **One early over-block.** The guard briefly blocked linked issue #13433, which has no comments, before it was narrowed to the evaluated PRs only.
- **Verification.** All 35 Sol jobs (60 passes) were verified as gpt-6.1-sol at xhigh, with exit 0 on every pass. Judges were Opus 5.5: one per PR plus one add-on, six in total.

## Conclusion (Part 3)

None of the five structural changes moves recall, calibration or lead choice clearly beyond pinned v10. The closest, E4 decomposed lenses, meets the pre-registered calibration bar by one PR on each test, does not beat v10 on recall or mean rank, and costs about eight times as much. **Recommendation: keep v10 (as pinned) as the GPT 6.1 main-review prompt; no production change from Part 3.** The user declined the E4 confirmation run, so Part 3 is closed.

# Part 4: GPT 6.1 Sol in its native harness, the Codex CLI (2026-10-01 to 2026-10-02)

**Goal.** Parts 1 to 3 ran GPT 6.1 Sol through Pi (`pi_job`). Part 4 asks whether the model does better in its native harness, the Codex CLI, with three prompt setups: no prompt optimization, pinned v10, and E5 (conclusion first, the cheapest Part 3 setup).

## Method

- **PRs.** The five final-check PRs from Parts 2 and 3: 13542, 13533, 13526, 13405 and 13569.
- **Codex runs.** `codex exec` (Codex CLI 0.159.2) with `-m gpt-6.1-sol`, `model_reasoning_effort=xhigh`, full access without approvals (as in Pi) and `--ignore-user-config`, so no personal plugins, MCP servers, hooks or memories applied. 15 runs, 4 at a time, driven by `tune/codex/run.py`.
- **Same inputs as Pi.** The goal was to change only the harness:
  - Developer instructions: the production `reviewer.md`, followed by the two AGENTS.md files that Pi loads from parent folders as project context.
  - First message: the brief and, for v10 and E5, the task file as file blocks, then `pi_job`'s own task text.
  - What still differs is the harness itself: Codex's base instructions, its tools (including built-in web search, which every run used, 49 searches in all) and its agent loop.
- **Pi pairs.** The existing Pi runs on the same PRs with the same prompts: untuned (`runs/sol61-review/`, Part 1 and 2), v10 (`runs/tune-v10/`) and E5 (`runs/bold-e5/`). No new Pi runs.
- **Verification.** Every Codex session rollout records the model and effort per turn. All 15 show only gpt-6.1-sol at xhigh, and all exited with 0.
- **Judging.** One blind judgement per PR covered seven reports: the three Codex runs, the three Pi runs and the Opus production report, under random letters, with runtime and setup self-labels redacted (`tune/JUDGE-CX.md`). The pool was the Part 3 pool, including the add-on judge's items, and the judges added new verified items as before. One new VALID item (13526) brings the pool to 24.
- **Discussion guard.** The `gh` guard was first on PATH. 5 of the 15 Codex runs tried to read their PR's own discussion (13 calls); the guard refused all of them. No web search or opened page touched an evaluated PR.

Cost for Codex is computed from the per-request token counts in each session rollout, at the list rates Pi uses for gpt-6.1-sol. Pi cost is Pi's own recorded cost. Opus is the Part 3 figure for these PRs.

## What it shows

- **The harness made no measurable difference to quality.** Codex against Pi, VALID found over the 5 PRs: 0 untuned, +1 with v10, +1 with E5. Part 2 measured the noise at 1 to 2 VALID per 5-PR set. Codex ranked above its Pi pair on 8 of 15 PR and setup pairs.
- **The prompt matters far more than the harness.** In both harnesses, v10 lifts GPT 6.1 from 13 to 19 or 20 VALID. Untuned GPT 6.1 ranks near the bottom in either harness.
- **Codex with v10 was the best configuration in this judging.** It found 20 of 24 VALID items, had the best mean rank (2.4) and ranked above Opus on 3 of 5 PRs. Its margin over Pi with v10 is within noise, and each cell is one run.
- **Codex was cheaper with v10 and slightly faster in all three setups.** v10 cost $1.65 against $2.25 per PR on Pi, with similar output. Untuned and E5 cost the same in both. Wall times are not strictly comparable: the Codex runs ran at night, the Pi runs in daytime alongside production.
- **Untuned GPT 6.1 in Codex did not shrink its own scope.** On 13526 the untuned Pi run treated itself as a boundary hunter and wrote a narrow report. The untuned Codex run, with the same instructions, did a full review. With one example this is a note, not a finding.
- **Opus** found 16 VALID items, ranked first on 13533 and tied first on 13405, and was last on 13569, where it missed the default-bar regression. This matches Part 3.

## Caveats

- One run per cell, and 5 PRs. Differences of 1 VALID or one rank place per PR are noise.
- The Pi runs are earlier runs, made at different times. Only the Codex runs are new.
- The Codex runs had built-in web search, which Pi's default tools lack (there, the model fetches sources through the shell). This is part of the harness difference being measured.
- Production tooling (`pi_job.py` jobs, `verify`, the coordinator's Sol checks) is built around Pi. Running Codex in production would need new tooling for starting jobs and verifying model and effort; `tune/codex/run.py` shows the pieces.

## Conclusion (Part 4)

GPT 6.1 Sol does about as well in the Codex CLI as in Pi, with every prompt tested. What lifts it is the v10 prompt, not the harness. Codex with v10 matched or slightly beat every other configuration here, including Opus, at under a third of Opus's list price, and cost less than Pi with v10. **Recommendation: no harness change on quality grounds. If the user wants the lower cost, Codex with v10 is a sound option, but moving production off Pi needs new job and verification tooling and the user's approval first.**

# The v10 prompt for GPT 6.1 Sol as main reviewer

v10 is the task prompt chosen in Part 2 of this eval, after 10 tuning iterations. It is 443 words long. GPT 6.1 Sol xhigh receives it after the PR's brief, on top of the production `reviewer.md` system prompt. The text below is the pinned copy, `tune/prompts/v10-pinned.md` (SHA-256 `6275e7e3d02e37ab556aa9a66a357c13bd5f322cae425499afb305c2a732b03f`, identical to `tune/prompts/v10.md`).

## What it did in the eval

- **Part 2.** It roughly doubled GPT 6.1's VALID findings on untouched validation PRs (16 against 8). In the blind final check on five unseen PRs, it found 20 VALID items, against 17 for Opus 5.5 and 17 for the untuned model.
- **Part 3.** None of five completely different review structures beat it clearly, so it was kept as pinned.
- **Part 4.** It worked as well in the Codex CLI as in Pi. Codex with v10 found 20 of 24 VALID items and had the best mean rank of the seven configurations judged, Opus included.

## Why it works

- **Recall:** steps 1 to 5 make the model check the change against the real system: premises on a real install, every entry point, each user population, the PR's claims against what actually changes, and tests that survive a broken change.
- **Calibration:** steps 7 and 8, and a severity scale anchored to the PR's own claims, stop the model from dismissing confirmed problems or giving untested fix advice.

## The prompt

```markdown
# Main technical review

You are the main technical reviewer for this PR. Do the full review your brief asks for: answer its questions, find the PR's defects, and recommend what should happen before merge. Save your report as `final.md` in your output directory.

Before writing findings, check the change against the real system, not just the unit:

1. **Premises:** for every guard or assumption in the new code, find what it evaluates to on a real Omarchy install (package dependencies, shipped defaults, installer, first run). If it is always true or always false, say what the PR then really does for everyone.
2. **Entry points:** for every way users reach the change (UI, each documented CLI form, config, installer, first run, update, migration), check the exact value that arrives and that the code handles it.
3. **Populations and states:** say what fresh installs, updated installs and customized configs each get, and trace the platform and session states the surrounding code handles.
4. **Claimed versus actual:** compare what the description says changes with what really changes for each population. An unstated default change, a claim that fails for some users, or behaviour that is wrong for a named group is a finding, not a product question.
5. **Tests:** mutate the main change (delete the call, drop the guard, hard-code the default) in a copy and run the PR's tests in review.py. A surviving mutant is a finding; so are tests that never touch the shipped defaults or the real path.
6. **Base:** label every finding as a regression, incomplete, or pre-existing.

7. **Before dismissing a confirmed mechanism** as user error, intended, pre-existing or a product question: if the repository's own docs, help or examples lead users there, it is the PR's defect; "intended" needs a quote from the PR description, a comment or the docs; "pre-existing" needs base behaving the same, and if the PR makes it reachable, likelier or permanent it is still this PR's finding.
8. **Fix advice:** when you suggest a fix or say an existing pattern would or would not fix it, check that claim like any other (read the pattern's code, or run it). Otherwise say it is untested.

Severity: High if the PR breaks something that works in base on a common setup or risks data or security; Medium if it does not deliver its claim for some population or misbehaves on a default or common setup, even with a small fix; Low for unusual states, manual edits, secondary test gaps and docs. Any High or Medium finding means "request changes". Order the findings by severity and state who reaches each.

End with the path of `final.md`.
```

Full results and method: see the eval report (`REPORT.md`), Parts 2 to 4.

# Duplicate PR detection (2026-09-29)

**Goal:** stop spending reviews on PRs that copy another open PR, and make sure every review knows about other open PRs that fix the same issue.

**Status: adopted 2026-09-29.** A dry run measured the effect, and the user approved the policy. Six duplicate notes are posted, and the driver rules take effect when batch v3-200-20260928 resumes. See "Decision and rollout" below.

## Why

On 2026-09-27 and 28, one account (author A) opened about 95 PRs through an AI agent pipeline (Cursor Agent, one PR per issue). Several fixed issues that other open PRs already fixed, and a few repeated the author's own earlier PRs. Our intake would have filled half a batch with them. See `batches/v3-200-20260928/queue.json`, `triage.author_held`.

## Method

`review-system/dupes.py scan` (read-only) compares each target PR with all 2,762 open PRs:
- **same_issue:** both PRs say they fix the same issue (GitHub closing references, or "Fixes/Closes/Resolves #N" in the body).
- **near_copy:** at least 80% of the later PR's added lines already appear in an earlier open PR, with at least 10 such lines.
- **same_area:** mostly the same files but few shared lines. Informational only.

Details:
- Pairs are found by shared issue, or by overlap of changed files (Jaccard at least 0.5). Files changed by 30 or more open PRs are ignored for this, and a PR that only touches such files is paired with PRs that touch exactly the same files.
- Added lines that appear in 10 or more of the compared diffs are ignored. This removes a stray fork commit that 88 author A PRs carry.

**Targets:** 306 PRs.

| Group | PRs |
|---|---|
| queued in v3-200-20260928 | 144 |
| posted by v3-200-20260928 | 54 |
| open PRs by author A | 108 |

Data: `data/prs.json`, `data/pairs.json`, `data/summary.json`, `policy-dryrun.json`.

## Results

**Near-copies: 7, all from author A.** Five repeat the author's own PR from the day before (containment 1.0: #13640, #13641, #13643, #13645, #13646). Two copy #13165 by another author (containment 0.93: #13477, #13645). No queued or posted PR outside author A is a near-copy.

**Hand check:**
- The first run used a 5-line minimum and flagged #12575 as a copy of #12254. The only shared lines were a 5-line test stub, so this was a false match, and the minimum was raised to 10.
- A sample of same-issue pairs was checked against the issue titles (#13229, #13374, #13367, #6475, #7868, #13265, #12197). All were correct matches.
- Some older PRs gained their closing reference later: for example #7497 from 2026-08-19 closes issue #13229 from 2026-09-25.

**Same issue, different code: 66 pairs.** Shared added lines were mostly 0 to 0.4, so these are competing fixes, not copies.

| | PRs with another open PR for the same issue | Our comment named it |
|---|---|---|
| Posted in v3-200-20260928 | 16 of 54 | 15 of 16 |
| Queued in v3-200-20260928 | 17 of 144 | not yet reviewed |

The existing process already cross-references competing PRs; the Sol hunter's related-PR search found them. The one miss is #13359: it did not name #6572, a much older PR for the same issue from 2026-08. Two queued PRs fix the same issue as each other: #13378 and #13446, issue #13349.

**Per-author volume (initial reviews only).** Follow-ups don't count toward this, since they respond to our own earlier reviews.
- Over 5 in this batch: author B 9 (8 already posted), author C 7, author D 6.
- Author B's 8 posted PRs (#13538 to #13545) were each a later, competing fix for an issue that already had an open PR.

## Policy (proposed after the dry run, adopted 2026-09-29)

1. **Skip near-copies:** at least 80% containment and at least 10 lines against an earlier open PR. Record the item as skipped with the earlier PR's number. In this data it catches exactly the repeated and copied PRs, and nothing else.
2. **Don't skip competing fixes.** Instead, put the detector's list of other open PRs for the same issue into the assignment brief, so every review names them, including old ones the hunter can miss (#13359).
   - Within one batch, when two queued PRs fix the same issue, review the earlier one and skip the later, and the review names both.
3. **Cap initial reviews at 5 per author per batch.** Follow-ups don't count. In this batch the cap would have held back 3 PRs from author B, 2 from author C and 1 from author D.

## Decision and rollout (2026-09-29)

The user approved the policy and asked that duplicates be flagged publicly even when they are not reviewed. There are four fixed note texts (`drafts/`), posted by `review-system/flags.py`. It remeasures every number at the PRs' current heads, and skips a PR that is closed, a draft, opted out, already reviewed or already flagged.

**Posted 2026-09-29.** Receipts are in `review-system/flags/registry.json`, and every body was verified after posting.

| PR | Note | Link |
|---|---|---|
| #13640 | B, same as #13480 | https://github.com/omacom/omarchy/pull/13640#issuecomment-5889076441 |
| #13641 | B, same as #13478 | https://github.com/omacom/omarchy/pull/13641#issuecomment-5889077623 |
| #13643 | B, same as #13476 | https://github.com/omacom/omarchy/pull/13643#issuecomment-5889078760 |
| #13645 | B, same as #13477 | https://github.com/omacom/omarchy/pull/13645#issuecomment-5889079919 |
| #13646 | B, same as #13474 | https://github.com/omacom/omarchy/pull/13646#issuecomment-5889081001 |
| #13685 | C, commit `2b4b0eba` carried by 88 PRs | https://github.com/omacom/omarchy/pull/13685#issuecomment-5889109615 |

#13477 (a copy of #13165) got no note, because it already had a full review from the previous batch.

**Driver rules,** active when the batch resumes (`batches/v3-200-20260928/rolling.py`, scan in `batches/v3-200-20260928/dupes/`):
- **Author cap:** at most 5 initial reviews per author per batch. Follow-ups don't count.
- **Near-copy:** posts note A or B, and skips the PR.
- **Same issue as another PR in this batch:** skips the later one. Note D is posted once the other PR's review is published. If the other PR is not reviewed after all, the skipped PR goes back into the queue.
- **Other open PRs for the same issue:** listed in `related-prs.json`, which is handed to the coordinator (`review_team.py assign --related`). The review names them in a collapsed block.
- **Intake:** also scans flagged PRs, so an opt-out reply to a note is seen.

**Simulation on the remaining queue (113 initial reviews):**
- 4 skipped by the author cap: #13496, #13446, #11477, #11475.
- 1 skipped as same-issue: #13444, same issue as #13544, which was already reviewed.
- 10 reviewed with a related-PR list.

# Readable review comments: a 1,500-character visible budget (2026-09-28)

**Goal:** make review comments short enough for a human to read, while keeping the full evidence available in collapsed blocks for maintainers and agents.

## Why

On PR #13298 (a BCM4350 Bluetooth coexistence fix), the author replied to the posted review ([comment](https://github.com/omacom/omarchy/pull/13298#issuecomment-5853837001)) that it was not a useful review. Three points:
- It opened with "No defect found in the normal dispatcher path" instead of the one real defect.
- It described its sandbox testing at length but did not share a runnable reproducer.
- For a hardware-specific patch, long source-level reasoning is no substitute for hardware testing.

The author reproduced and fixed the one defect the review raised.

Comment length had also grown over time, measured on posted comments:

| Batch | Posted | Median length | Longest 10% start at | Median "Verified" section |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| v3-25b (2026-09-24) | 25 | 4,817 | 7,264 | 453 |
| v3-200 (2026-09-24) | 200 | 5,506 | 7,913 | 509 |
| v3-200 (2026-09-27) | 215 | 6,672 | 9,468 | 950 |

Before the change, across all 480 posted reviews: median visible length 6,048 characters; 0% within 1,500; 7% open with an outcome line; 0.4% use collapsed blocks (`scores/live.json`, "before").

## What changed

The rules, applied to reviews drafted from the date of this report:
- **Visible budget:** at most 1,500 characters outside `<details>` blocks, including the heading and footer. `check-comment` measures it exactly and gives the number to the editorial check. The batch driver also holds any draft over 1,500 as a backstop.
- **Order:** `**Outcome:**` in one sentence first (the most important defect, or "No defects found"). Then each defect in 2–4 sentences, with one Suggested change sentence.
- **Collapsed blocks:**
  - a Reproducer block for every reproduced finding: runnable, preferably as a test case in the PR's own test file, with its actual output;
  - a Details block for sequences and evidence;
  - Verified (at most 5 bullets) and optional notes (at most 3) go in the collapsed blocks.
- **Scope:** one short Test scope sentence in Review information, such as "source code and sandbox tests only; not tested on hardware". The PR is not explained back to its author.
- **Reviewers** save a postable reproducer and its real output for every finding they reproduce. Illustrative output is not allowed.

The full text changes are in `requirements.diff` (comment requirements) and `compliance.diff` (editorial checker).

## Check against the new rules

The same #13298 review, run through the new editorial check (Opus 5.5 Medium, fresh session each time; `scores/editorial-checks.json`):

| Draft | Visible chars | Verdict | Issues |
|---|---|---|---|
| As posted (old template) | 7,728 | revise | 8: over budget, opens with what passed, Verified visible, no reproducer block, visible sequence, … |
| New template, draft 1 | 1,211 | revise | 2: missing Review information heading, two-sentence Outcome |
| New template, draft 2 | 1,222 | revise | 1: an optional note without a stated benefit |
| New template, final | 1,222 | **pass** | 0 |

The drafts are in `drafts/`. The reproducer in the new-template draft is illustrative: it was built from the review's recorded sequence and not run. Under the new rules a real review pastes its sandbox output.

## Live results

`measure.py --cutoff <time the rules went live>` compares posted reviews before and after the change: median and 90th-percentile visible length, the share within 1,500, the share opening with an outcome line, and the share using collapsed blocks. Results are written to `scores/live.json`.

First measurement, 2026-09-29: the 54 reviews posted by batch v3-200-20260928 (rules live from 2026-09-28 22:01 UTC, the time in that batch's `rules-live-utc.txt`):

| | Before (480 reviews) | After (54 reviews) |
|---|---|---|
| Visible length, median | 6,048 | 1,486 |
| Visible length, 90th percentile | 8,662 | 1,499 |
| Within 1,500 visible | 0% | 100% |
| Opens with an outcome line | 7% | 100% |

**Goal:** bring the Sol hunter close to the Opus xhigh hunter in up to 5 prompt iterations.

## Tuning set (10 PRs, reference = 66 valid issues from an Opus xhigh hunter)

Scores are in `evals/sol-hunter-tuning-20260927/scores/<version>/`. Prompts are in `evals/sol-hunter-tuning-20260927/prompts/`.

| v4 (production) | 32/66 | 22/35 | 1 | 1 | – | 9.0 |

| v9: standalone fixture and test issues, input shapes, receipts | 55/66 | 28/34 | 5 | 2 | 29 | 35.3 |

v10 and v11 add the fixes from the v8 and v9 judges. Their main changes:
- Merge against the other PR's own diff or merge-base (the cause of both of v9's WRONG issues).
- The second pass may delete a finding only when a source line disproves it.
- A worksheet row that shows a problem must become an issue.
- Weak-test issues must name a plausible mutant.

v11 was not scored on the tuning set. It went straight to the held-out check.

## Held-out check (5 PRs from the 2026-09-24 batch that no tuning round used)

The judge was blind: 3 runs per PR under anonymous ids, every issue verified against the pinned source, and the pool of valid issues built from all runs. Details are in `scores/`; the unblinded totals are in `scores/unblinded-totals.json`.

| Config | VALID found (of 25) | Partial | Unique VALID | MINOR | WRONG | Coverage honest | Min/PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opus 5.5 xhigh, production prompt | 24 | 1 | 1 | 20 | 0 | 10/10 | 16.2 |
| **Sol xhigh, v11 plus second pass** | **22** | 1 | 0 | 22 | **0** | 9/10 | 27.0 |
| Sol xhigh, production prompt (v4) | 14 | 2 | 0 | 11 | 1 | 10/10 | 6.8 |

- **v11 against Opus.** v11 found 22 of the 24 valid issues Opus found. It missed two:
  - 12425: reset toasts bypass Do Not Disturb through the default app name.
  - 12167: the PR targets the stale `dev` branch.

  v11 raised no valid issue Opus lacked, and neither made a WRONG claim.
- **v11 against production Sol.** Valid issues rose from 14 to 22, and WRONG fell from 1 to 0. MINOR noise doubled, to Opus's level. Time rose about 4×.
- **Caveat.** The judge counted weak-test items as VALID when the PR's own tests pass with its main change removed. Under the per-PR judges' original ratings, the pool is 22: Opus 22, v11 19 plus 1 partial, production 14 plus 1 partial.

## Costs

- **Sol:** no Claude usage. v11 takes about 27 min per PR in two passes. In tuning it ranged from 19 to 79 min; one PR (12252) is an outlier at 49 + 30.
- **Opus xhigh as hunter:** $28.90 for 5 PRs (about $5.80 per PR) of Claude usage, 16 min per PR.

## Deploying v11 (not done; needs a decision)

1. Replace `prompts/sol-hunter.md` with `v11.md`, retitled as production.
2. Add the second pass. `pi_job.py --hunt` would resume the job once with `second-pass-v5.md` after the first pass exits, so coordinators need no new step. Alternatively, coordinators run `pi_job.py resume`.
3. The hunter now runs longer than the Opus review (27 min against about 20), so coordinators wait on it more often. Consider a cap, for example stopping the second pass after 20 minutes.

## Effort check

v11 plus its second pass, same 5 held-out PRs, judged blind against the same verified pool (`scores-effort/`, `blind-mapping-effort.json`). Costs are list-price token costs from the Pi session logs (`cost.py`), or `total_cost_usd` for Opus.

# What does Sol add over Opus alone? (pilot, 5 PRs per arm, 2026-09-26)

Judgements are in `arm1-judgement.json` (blind), `arm2-judgement.json` and `arm3-judgement.json`. Nothing was posted.

## Arm 1: coordinator draft, Opus only (A) vs Opus plus Sol verifier verdicts (B)

PRs: 12524, 13189, 13121, 12413 and 12271.

| | A (Opus only) | B (Opus + Sol verdicts) |
|---|---|---|
| Correct claims | 206 of 214 (96.3%) | 202 of 207 (97.6%) |
| Wrong or overstated claims | 8 | 5 |
| Valid findings unique to the draft | 22 | 19 |

- **Where B helped:** almost all of its gain is on 13189, where it removed all 5 of A's errors. The orchestrator checked on GitHub that the Chromium version is in issue #13188, not in the PR body.
- **Where B hurt:** on 12524 and 12271 it was equal or worse. It re-marked verified facts as "not verified" and dropped findings and evidence.
- **Verdict:** no measurable accuracy gain. The verdicts make the coordinator slightly more precise and more hedged.

## Arm 2: Sol challenges the published comment

PRs: 12569, 12524, 12271, 12510 and 13189.

- **Scale:** 303 claims checked, 35 flagged.
  - Real errors: 5 flags, from 2 distinct mistakes.
  - Nitpicks: 27.
  - False alarms: 3.
- **Known errors caught:** 2 of 3. It caught 12569 "only output" and 13189's missing third route, but not 12524 "safe to retry".
- **Filter:** keeping only WRONG verdicts backed by a sealed run or an upstream line leaves 6 flags, of which 2 are real.
- **Cost:** 13.5 min per PR.

## Arm 3: Sol adjacent-risk hunter (brief only, no Opus output)

PRs: 12220, 12413, 12545, 12510 and 12635.

- **Known targets:** it found 2 of the 5 that Opus's first pass missed (12220 package_defaults, 12413 version:2). It missed 12545 locate, 12510 device_name and 12635 401/403 with cache. The misses happened because Sol read "don't review the PR's own logic" as excluding edge paths.
- **Other issues:** 13 in total; 12 correct, 2 new. Both new ones are merge-coordination notes about open PRs:
  - 12510 plus #11874 gives double Thunderbolt prompts. The orchestrator checked that #11874 is open and adds Thunderbolt authorization scripts.
  - 12635 plus #12651 and others gives duplicate OpenCode Go collectors.
- **Errors:** 1 wrong finding, on 12635, which rested on the PR's own false comment about OpenCode storage.
- **Cost:** 7.7 min per PR. It needs no Opus output, so it can run in parallel with Opus.
- **Prompt fixes proposed:**
  1. Absent fields, 401/403 responses, missing keys and cache fallbacks are in scope.
  2. The package-collision check runs in both directions, and always includes the examples the PR's own comments name.
  3. Read the argument validation of every helper the new code calls.
  4. No "verified" when a premise rests on the PR's own comments about a dependency.
  5. Report each fixture or registration gap as its own issue.
  6. Keep the related-open-PR step.

## Reading

- The verifier does not measurably improve the posted text.
- The challenger catches the kind of error that actually reaches the public comment, but needs strict filtering.
- The hunter adds cheap, parallel discovery of a kind Opus misses, with modest recall that the prompt fixes should improve.
- Sample: 5 PRs per arm, so these results are indicative.

## Arm 3 follow-up: hunter v2 (2026-09-26)

Judgement is in `arm3v2-judgement.json`. The holdout targets were pre-registered in `holdout-targets.json` before any v2 output existed.

**Tuned 5 (v1 → v2):**
- Known targets: 2/5 → 4/5. `device_name` is still missed.
- 12510 `--exec` defect: missed → found.
- Wrong issues: 1 → 1.
- Scope drift: 1 → 0.
- Time: 7.7 → 8.5 min per PR.

**Holdout 5:** 10 of 19 boundary targets found under the strict count (10 of 18 if the likely-invalid 12268 F2 is removed), and 14 of 29 under the lenient count. It found 3 valid new issues.

**All 10 runs:**
- 61 issues, of which 59 are correct (96.7%).
- 7 valid new issues, mostly conflicts with other open PRs. The orchestrator confirmed 13189 B4: open #12971's test runs `cmp` on chromium-flags.conf with no PCI stub.
- `coverage.json` over-claims "checked" in 4 of 10 runs.

**v3 prompt:** `tasks/hunter-v3.md` adds the judge's fixes and has not been run yet:
1. Test absent fields, not just empty ones.
2. Report premise contradictions, reading the specific upstream code.
3. A per-item file:line for every "checked" coverage entry, with no templates.
4. One issue per list.
5. Check docs and metadata examples, and every group-creating package in the same list.
6. Report fewer issues when the rest are immaterial.

## Arm 3 follow-up: hunter v3 (2026-09-26)

Judgement is in `arm3v3-judgement.json`. It uses the same method and targets as v2.

| | v2 | v3 |
|---|---|---|
| Tuned targets | 4/5 | 4/5 |
| Holdout strict | 10/19 | 12/19 (10/19 if two borderline matches are read strictly) |
| Issues | 61 | 51 |
| Correct | 96.7% | 100% |
| Valid new | 7 | 6 |
| Honest coverage files | 6/10 | 8/10 |
| Min per PR | 9.1 | 10.9 |

**Targeted fixes:** only partly effective.
- Still missed: `device_name` (seen, then judged acceptable), plocate (skipped), and Chromium's VaapiOnNvidiaGPUs.
- 12510 regressed: 2 issues, packaging gaps lost, and a false "checked" on pruning. The orchestrator confirmed at pinned head 44d34868 that `bin/omarchy-thunderbolt-check:114-118` only echoes `pruned:`. The current PR head has since added the `unset`.

**Remaining fixes proposed by the judge:**
1. A cross-PR conflict confirmed at file:line goes into `issues`, not `limits`.
2. Report any absent field that causes a silent skip.
3. Always inventory the PKGBUILD, package lists and fixture lists.
4. Read the sysusers file of every direct entry in the same package list.
5. For premise checks, read the consumer's source (for example Chromium) as well as the dependency's.

**Reading:**
- v3 is the most precise version so far, with recall roughly the same as v2.
- Differences between single runs per PR are within noise: 12510 and the loss of the #12971 conflict could be run-to-run variance.
- Further prompt tuning on these same 10 PRs risks overfitting.

## Arm 4: Opus 5.5 xhigh checks the final comment against its own evidence (2026-09-26)

**Setup:** same PRs as arm 2. A fresh session was given the original Opus output folder; the reviewer's live context was not available. Judgement is in `arm4-judgement.json`.

| | Opus self-check | Sol challenger |
|---|---|---|
| Flags | 31 | 35 |
| Distinct real errors | 5 (2 known + 3 new minor) | 2 (the same 2 known) |
| Harmful false alarms | fewer: the main one was "head moved", a post-hoc timing artifact | 2 that would weaken the 12524 blocker |
| Known errors caught | 2/3 | 2/3 |
| Minutes per PR | 7.2 | 13.5 |
| Cost | $2.27 per PR (Claude usage) | Codex subscription, not metered |

- **The "WRONG only" filter does not work for Opus.** Opus labels most real errors OVERSTATED, so the coordinator has to triage every flag: about 6 per PR, of which about 1 is real.
- **Where the errors come from:** most real errors are losses during synthesis. The orchestrator confirmed that 12510's report had `TAG+="systemd"` and the comment dropped it. 12569's error comes from an inconsistency inside the Opus report itself.
- **Missed by both:** the 12524 retry overgeneralization.

- **12220:** `package_defaults` omits the new unit.
- **12413:** `validate_config` accepts `version:2`.

- **12545 headline:** `docker`/`locate` accepted as the primary group.

- **13121 lead bug:** pin/hide erases `drawerReversed`.
- **12385 only section:** rated severity "none".
- **12510 scope:** most of it arrived only via follow-up.

## Conclusion

- **Unique value:** only 5/117 published findings (4%) came solely from Sol, and most are secondary. Opus's first pass alone held 96% of published findings and every lead finding.
- **Confirmation:** Sol confirmed 67 findings independently, which supports "independently confirmed" labels.
- **Follow-ups:** 37 more findings reached Sol only through follow-ups built around Opus's report. That is weak evidence of independence.
- **Error load:** Sol missed 6/20 lead findings, made 8 false claims and often miscalibrated severity. None was published.
- **Cost:** about 14 min of Sol time per PR.
- **Recommendation:** if Sol is kept, it looks better suited to being a targeted verifier than a parallel full reviewer.

# Astra vs Sol (2026-09-26): 40 runs on Sol's 5 worst PRs

**PRs:** 12545, 12271, 13121, 12385 and 12510.

**Configurations:** GPT 6 Astra at medium, high and xhigh, and GPT 6 Sol at xhigh (baseline). Each ran as a full parallel reviewer (from the brief) and as a verifier (with the same packets), under the current instructions. All runs passed the model and thinking-level check.

**Scoring:** done blind, per PR and mode, reusing the earlier eval methods. Details are in `scoring.json` and `scores/`, and the anonymisation mapping is `blind-mapping.json`.

## Full parallel reviewer (32 published findings)

| Config | Found / weak / missed | Leads | False claims | Severity errors | Median min |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Astra medium | 14 / 9 / 9 | 1/5 | 0 | 4 | 5.0 |
| Astra high | 16 / 8 / 8 | 1/5 | 0 | 6 | 8.1 |
| Astra xhigh | 13 / 10 / 9 | 1/5 | 0 | 4 | 14.3 |
| Sol xhigh | 13 / 3 / 16 | 2/5 | 0 | 2 | 10.2 |

- No configuration beats the old Sol first pass on these PRs (16/32, 1/5 leads).
- All of them fall far short of Opus's first pass (20/20 leads in the original sample).
- Astra repeated the old Sol failures on 12545, 12271 and 13121, and also on 12385, which the new Sol run now gets right.

## Verifier (32 published findings)

| Config | Verified | Refuted wrongly | Unverifiable | Citations exact | Errors | Median min |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Astra medium | 31 | 0 | 0 | 44/44 | 3 | 8.5 |
| Astra high | 31 | 0 | 0 | 46/46 | 2 | 14.1 |
| Astra xhigh | 31 | 0 | 0 | 48/48 | 1 | 21.2 |
| Sol xhigh | 30 | 0 | 1 | 42/43 | 3 | 8.2 |

- **Leads:** every verifier verified all 5 leads.
- **Findings missing from the packet:** none recovered them. 12510 `device_name` and 12545 `locate` were both missed, and every adjacent-risk pass said "nothing further found".
- **Astra's lean:** it rates items lower than published (14–19 per level, against Sol's 6). It cut the 12271 and 12545 leads, where Sol held or raised their severity.
- **Astra xhigh:** strongest evidence (namespace, offscreen Quickshell and fault-injection runs), at about 2.5 times Sol's time.

## Orchestrator checks

- Confirmed that the 13121 packet contains a pasted `<function_results>` fragment (line 156). `pi_job.py start --verify` now refuses packets that contain tool-transcript markers.
- Confirmed that Astra medium's 12510 report claims "no opt-out command", although the units carry a negated `ConditionPathExists` opt-out.

## Conclusion

- No GPT model is worth running as a full parallel reviewer. Opus remains the only discovery reviewer.
- As the verifier, Astra medium is equivalent to Sol xhigh on yield and speed, slightly better on citations, and worse on keeping lead severity.
- Sample: 5 hard PRs per configuration. Treat the differences as indicative.

## Automated AI review

> **Community review:** Independent automated community review, unaffiliated with the Omarchy team, intended to help prepare PRs for their review.

No defect found in the normal dispatcher path at `4e8afe85`. One narrow ownership-marker case can still overwrite a policy the dispatcher did not set, and a few test and logging notes follow. Everything below comes from source reading and a sandbox with a stubbed `iw`. Nothing ran on the target hardware.

**Verified:**
- **Vendor request and reply.** The request bytes match brcmfmac's `struct brcmf_vndr_dcmd_hdr` in Linux v7.2 (`vendor.h`):
  - get: `(262, 256, 20, 0, 0) + "ver\0"`
  - set: `(263, 13, 20, 1, 0) + "btc_mode\0" + LE 4`

  The parser accepts the kernel's actual reply layout (DATA, then LEN, plain attribute types). Broadcom's `wlioctl_defs.h` defines 4 as parallel and 5 as hybrid. brcmfmac's own coexistence code writes `btc_params`, never `btc_mode`, so the driver itself never overwrites it (a firmware reload returns it to the default).
- **Scope guards.** Other models, or missing DMI, exit in bash with no `iw` call. A MacBookPro14,1 with different firmware gets one read-only `ver` query and no `btc_mode` access. A different vendor, device, revision or driver gets no `iw` call.
- **Packaging and dispatch.** `omarchy-settings` copies `etc/` with `cp -a` under makepkg's `umask 0022`, so the file ships 0755 root:root. That passes NetworkManager's dispatcher permission check (root-owned, not group/other-writable, owner-executable). NetworkManager rescans `dispatcher.d` on each event and runs scripts one at a time, so a newly installed file takes effect at the next event, and the script never runs concurrently with itself. `NetworkManager.service` enables the dispatcher service through `Also=`, on fresh installs and on the quattro upgrade path. `iw` arrives through `wireless-regdb` and `python` through `python-gobject`, both in `install/omarchy-base.packages`. The package build was not run; this chain comes from reading the PKGBUILD and makepkg.
- **Failure handling.** A missing `iw`, a hung `iw` (ended by `timeout=2` after about 2.07 s), firmware errors, empty replies and device removal all exit 0.
- **Test.** The new test passes at this head (6 `ok -` lines) and fails on the base tree, where the dispatcher does not exist. It caught 12 of 15 diagnostic mutants of the dispatcher.

### A stale ownership marker can restore 5 over another writer's 4

If a dispatcher event arrives after the card was unbound or removed, the sysfs `vendor` read (dispatcher lines 57-59) raises before any marker logic. `main()` catches it and exits 0, and `/run/omarchy-bcm4350-coexistence/<iface>` stays. A firmware hang during the run keeps the marker the same way. After a rebind, the firmware is back at 5 and usually the next event clears or reuses the marker correctly. The wrong write needs a second writer that sets exactly 4:

```text
up on 2.4 GHz            write 4, marker created
card unbound, then down   sysfs read fails, marker kept
rebind                    firmware back at 5
another tool sets 4       (while on 5 GHz)
next up on 5 GHz          marker present, mode 4 -> writes 5
```

Reproduced with the production script and a stubbed `iw`. With the other writer's 4 already set at a 2.4 GHz `up`, the marker also survives, and the next off-2.4 event writes 5. Neither write happens without the stale marker.

**Impact:** a single write of the hybrid default while off 2.4 GHz, outside the 2.4 GHz case the issue describes. It contradicts the line 82 comment and the docs' "only if `/run/omarchy-bcm4350-coexistence/` records that it applied parallel mode". It needs a second writer of `btc_mode`, such as an administrator's own earlier workaround script; nothing at the quattro tip or in the related PRs writes `btc_mode`. A stale marker needs the card to be re-registered with fresh firmware while the marker exists and before an event clears it: for example a manual rebind, a module reload, brcmfmac's crash reset, or its resume re-probe when the sleep-time `down` runs late. Open PRs #7180, #7333, #12314 and #12688 unbind and rebind this card around every suspend, which would put every suspend taken on 2.4 GHz into this race; how often NetworkManager's `down` loses it was not measured.

**Suggested change:** record the interface's `ifindex` in the marker when taking ownership, and drop a marker whose `ifindex` differs from the live interface before deciding anything. Linux assigns a new `ifindex` on each netdev registration, so a rebind, crash reset or module reload changes it. A prototype of this passed all of the marker sequences above plus the normal-behaviour checks. The PR's own test was not run against it; its fake sysfs would need an `ifindex` file. Deleting the marker when the device node is missing is simpler but does not cover the firmware-hang case.

### Minor notes

- **Optional test improvement:** removing the `if current == 4:` restore guard (dispatcher line 83) still passes the test, because the independent-policies block drops ownership with a `reapply` on 2.4 GHz before changing band. Apply on 2.4 GHz, then change the mode to 2 with no event, then send `down`; expecting no write and mode 2 fails that mutant.
- **Optional test improvement:** the test's `iw` stub sends LEN before DATA and sets the nested flag on DATA (test lines 75-77). The kernel sends DATA then LEN with plain types. The production parser handles both, but a parser that matched only the kernel's plain types failed the test. Emitting DATA then LEN with plain attribute types, as brcmfmac does, would test the real layout.
- **Optional:** on MacBookPro14,1, handled events for interfaces without a PCI device (for example Docker bridges or USB network adapters) log `BCM4350: coexistence quirk skipped (FileNotFoundError)`, which reads like a failure. Returning silently when `/sys/class/net/<iface>/device/vendor` is absent would avoid this.
- **Optional:** the dispatcher is package-owned in `/etc` and replaced on upgrade, and a deliberately chosen mode 5 cannot be told apart from the default, so there is no persistent opt-out. NetworkManager also reads `/usr/lib/NetworkManager/dispatcher.d/`, where `/etc` takes precedence and a `/dev/null` symlink masks a script. Shipping it there would give administrators that standard mask, at the cost of a PKGBUILD install line and a departure from the `etc/` pattern.
- **Related:** open PR #7644 targets Broadcom Bluetooth audio dropouts on Macs by other means (codec cap, btusb autosuspend) and touches none of these files. This head merges cleanly with the quattro tip and with #7644, #12314 and #12688.

**Test scope:** head `4e8afe85`, merge base `7b336b1b` on `quattro`. Source reading of the dispatcher, the omarchy-settings PKGBUILD and makepkg, NetworkManager's dispatcher (main and 1.58.1), Linux v7.2 brcmfmac and iw 6.17. Runs in a sandbox with no network and an empty `/sys`: the PR test, 15 dispatcher mutants, and scenario runs of the production script with sysfs, DMI and `/run` paths redirected and `iw` stubbed from the brcmfmac and iw sources. No real hardware, NetworkManager or `iw` was used. Not established: whether the final script's 5→4 write and 4→5 restore ran on hardware (the PR describes a run on already-repaired hardware), and any Wi-Fi throughput or latency cost of parallel mode, which the issue does not measure.

**AI process:** Opus 5.5 Medium coordination and synthesis, Opus 5.5 Xhigh technical review and final fact check, GPT 6 Sol Xhigh search for related issues, Opus 5.5 Medium editorial check.
