retro_themes.method: Every coordinator writes a short retrospective after posting. A model read all 225 from this batch and grouped what they say; the counts were spot-checked against the text and are conservative (a review is counted only when its retrospective clearly says it).
retro_themes.trend: The same few tooling problems recur from the first hour of the batch to the last. What changes is how they are handled: early retrospectives describe them as new bugs, later ones treat the workaround as an expected step. The self-check stays valuable throughout.

themes.title: The self-check catches wrong or overstated claims before posting
themes.summary: Re-reading the draft against the evidence repeatedly found false or exaggerated statements, including some that came from the reviewer's own report. They were fixed before the comment went out.

themes.title: Running the main review and the boundary hunt in parallel
themes.summary: Starting both at once saved time, and the two independent efforts cross-checked each other's main conclusions.

themes.title: The hunter finds other open pull requests that clash with this one
themes.summary: It often turned up other open pull requests touching the same code, which the main reviewer had not looked for, and these became verified findings in the comment.

themes.title: Running real code in a sandbox turns guesses into observed facts
themes.summary: Reviewers built small working reproductions (compiling upstream code, running a real terminal session, loading the program offscreen) so a claim about behaviour was something they had watched happen.

themes.title: Stable IDs for earlier findings make follow-ups faster
themes.summary: When the brief labelled each earlier finding (F1, F2, …), the follow-up could say what happened to each one directly instead of re-describing the earlier review.

themes.title: Moving the reviewer's files breaks its code checkouts
themes.summary: A late step relocates the reviewer's working folder, which breaks the extra code checkouts it made for testing; they had to be repaired by hand again and again.

themes.title: No shared tool turns the draft into a web preview
themes.summary: Nearly every review wrote its own small, throwaway converter to preview the Markdown draft as HTML.

themes.title: Reading the team's full job history produces an oversized dump
themes.summary: Coordinators opened the whole history file just to see the current job; reading only the needed fields would avoid it.

themes.title: Checking on the hunt can reveal its headline too early
themes.summary: The status check for the hunter prints a one-line summary of what it found, so the coordinator could see it before the independent main review was finished.

themes.title: The reviewer is sometimes blocked from saving its own report
themes.summary: The coordinator then copied the report out of the reviewer's hand-off message, often enough that it became a documented routine.

themes.title: Asking an intake script for help starts a real run
themes.summary: The script has no usage help, so the help flag was read as a folder name and started a run that had to be stopped.

themes.title: Teams share one GitHub request allowance
themes.summary: Searches for related pull requests occasionally hit the hourly limit mid-review and had to wait or use a slower route.

themes.title: Shortening a report into a comment tends to drop qualifiers
themes.summary: Words that limit a claim to a condition, such as "only when X", were the most common loss, turning a narrow, accurate finding into a broader one. The self-check exists largely to catch this.

themes.title: State each finding's impact explicitly
themes.summary: The editorial check repeatedly sent drafts back because a finding had no clearly labelled impact; writing it in from the start saves a round.

themes.title: Describe facts, not merge or severity verdicts
themes.summary: Words like "blocking" or "Minor:" were sent back: the review describes what it found and leaves the decision to the maintainers.

themes.title: Pull requests by contributors who opted out are left unmentioned
themes.summary: When a related pull request came from someone who opted out, teams chose not to mention it in the public comment; there is no written rule yet.

themes.title: Small checks run outside the sandbox tool, and disclosed
themes.summary: Reviewers disclosed running small commands (a syntax check, a lookup of an installed program) directly on the host on their own test files. None touched the pull request's code.

themes.title: Merge tests confined to the reviewer's own disposable copy
themes.summary: To test whether two pull requests merge cleanly, reviewers wrote to their own throwaway copy of the code rather than the shared source, which the rules allow.

themes.title: The reviewer fell back to an older model mid-run
themes.summary: Twice the main reviewer switched to an older Opus model near the end of a long run, and model verification caught it before posting. Once a fresh reviewer redid the work; the other time the replacement fell back as well, and the review was posted with that disclosed.

improvements.title: From retrospectives to fixes (2026-09-28)
improvements.summary: The retrospectives of the batch were read for problems that kept coming back. Each one got a fix, a reason, and a detector. The same detector is run on reviews dispatched before and after the fix, so the page shows whether the problem actually went away.
improvements.applied_note: Fixes are prepared and tested on copies, then applied by the review system's own operator between reviews.

items.problem: Moving the reviewer's files breaks its code checkouts
items.why: When a reviewer finishes, its private folder is moved into the review folder. Git keeps absolute paths for extra checkouts, so they pointed at the old place and every reviewer had to repair them by hand before continuing.
items.fix: The move now rewrites the paths git keeps, right after moving, including the record kept by a repo outside the folder when a checkout belongs to it (follow-up applied 23:47:54 the same evening). Tested on real worktrees and shared clones: broken before, working after, and safe from git's cleanup.

items.problem: Checking on the hunt revealed its conclusion too early
items.why: The two reviews are meant to be independent until both are done. The status check printed the hunter's latest message, so the coordinator could see where the hunt was going while the main review was still running.
items.fix: The hunter's message stays hidden until its output is released after both reviews finish (it can still be shown on request).

items.problem: Asking a script for help started a real run
items.why: The intake script took any first argument as a folder name, so '--help' started a real fetch from GitHub that then had to be stopped.
items.fix: '--help' now prints usage, and nothing that looks like an option can start a run.

items.problem: Every review wrote its own HTML preview script
items.why: There was no shared tool, so coordinators kept writing small converters, each slightly different and each a place for rendering mistakes.
items.fix: One shared renderer, which also shows collapsed evidence blocks the way GitHub does, and a line in the runbook pointing to it.

measure.basis: reviews with their own preview script

items.problem: The reviewer was blocked from saving its own report
items.why: Claude Code asks subagents to return findings as text rather than write report files, so some saves were refused.
items.fix: Already handled on 2026-09-27: the reviewer hands its report back as text and a tool saves it verbatim with a provenance record.

items.problem: Unclear whether a comment may mention a PR by someone who opted out
items.why: With no written rule, coordinators left such PRs out even when they mattered, for example a real merge conflict.
items.fix: Decided: an opt-out stops reviews of that person's own pull requests only. Their other pull requests may be mentioned like any other.
